cards.title: Pre-diagnosis rules: change history, time horizon, conversion latency
cards.summary: Three checks to run before touching a Google Ads account that looks like it's underperforming.
cards.use_when: Before diagnosing or editing Google Ads when a store's revenue or ROAS appears to have dropped.
steps: Check change history first. If anyone (you, a teammate, the client, another agency) recently tweaked settings, bids, budgets, campaign structure or the website, assume that change is the cause before running any audit. Never make new changes on top of unexplained recent changes.
Extend the time horizon. Avoid diagnosing on a 1-day read; zoom out as far as the account's conversion volume allows so you are not making decisions off small-sample noise.

Check conversion latency. In Google Ads, conversions are attributed back to the click date, not the purchase date. So the last 3–4 days always look terrible on default conversion and ROAS columns, in every account.
Build a custom column using 'conversions by conversion time' (conversions credited to the day of purchase) to get a real-time read on the last few days.
Only after those three checks should you start level-one diagnosis; otherwise you risk changing a healthy account and pushing it into a worse position.
caveats: The speaker states last 3–4 days always look bad in every account — this is their framing of default attribution behavior, not a benchmark.
Redesigning the account (or multiple changes at once) risks a learning-phase reset that deepens the decline.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Level-one business check: cross-channel spend weighting and the revenue equation
cards.summary: Determine whether a revenue dip is even a Google problem by checking media mix share and which revenue-equation lever moved.
cards.use_when: When a store reports a revenue or efficiency drop and you must decide whether to investigate Google Ads, Meta/other channels, or the website first.
steps: Establish the media mix by spend share. If Google is only ~10% of spend (e.g., 90% Meta), a top-line revenue dip is very unlikely to be a Google issue — start elsewhere.
If spend is more evenly split (e.g., 65% Meta / 35% Google), still do due diligence on both, but start with the higher-spend platform.

Ask what else changed outside Google: did a promotion end, was there a creative refresh on Meta, did the offer change, did the business change something material? Get the client to confirm anything you're not across.
Decompose the revenue equation: Revenue = Conversion Rate × Average Order Value × Sessions. Identify which of the three fell.

Interpret the lever: AOV down points to product mix / upsell-cross-sell changes; conversion rate down points to landing page, offer or audience; sessions down points to a traffic source losing click volume.
Reconcile platform attribution against true business KPIs (revenue, profit contribution, MER/AMER) to distinguish a real business decline from a tracking or attribution error.
caveats: The speaker notes the majority of accounts they see skew to Meta — this is their client-base observation, not a universal rule.
If Google holds majority spend, run the Google drill first even though the general sequence favours the biggest spender.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Check seasonality against a forecast before diagnosing
cards.summary: Use forecasting to rule out expected seasonal dips so you don't run a multi-hour diagnostic on normal fluctuation.
cards.use_when: When a store's revenue dips and you need to decide whether the decline is a real anomaly or expected seasonality before investing time in root-cause work.
steps: Maintain a forecast for the business so each period has an expected revenue range rather than a single number.
When a dip appears, compare actual against the forecast for that period. If the dip is in line with expected seasonality, stop — do not run a diagnostic process to 'fix' something that was predicted.
If the dip is outside forecast, proceed to the cross-channel and revenue-equation checks.
Where forecasting is absent, treat any seasonal dip as a real problem and expect to burn hours diagnosing a fluctuation that will recur.
Keep the forecast updated so the comparison is meaningful over time.
caveats: The speaker's process treats an expected seasonal dip as requiring no action — this depends on the forecast being accurate; a bad forecast mislabels real declines as seasonality.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Prioritise diagnosis by spend: top-5 campaigns only
cards.summary: Ignore low-spend campaigns during diagnosis because even a doubled result there cannot move the business.
cards.use_when: When drilling into a Google Ads account to find the cause of a material business decline.
steps: In the campaign tab, sort by cost descending so the highest-spend campaigns sit at the top.

Do not spend diagnostic time below the top five campaigns by spend. Example: a campaign at 10% of budget doubling performance moves the business ~5%, and if Google is only 40% of your media mix, that is single-digit impact.
Theoretically a small campaign could be the cause, but the speaker argues it is unlikely; start where the impact is and work down only after the likely causes are cleared.
Ask the client's specific complaint against this lens: if it's a 10% ROAS decline on the fifth-biggest spender while business-level KPIs are up, it probably does not need investigating at all.
caveats: The 10%-budget and 40%-media-mix numbers are illustrative examples, not thresholds to apply as hard rules.
This is the speaker's prioritisation heuristic; a small campaign can occasionally be the root cause.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: 90–180 day weekly overview scan before drilling into campaigns
cards.summary: A five-minute account-level scan of weekly metrics to find the inflection point and which metric changed.
cards.use_when: When starting the Google Ads portion of a diagnosis, before looking at individual campaigns.
steps: Set date range to the last 90–180 days and switch to a weekly view.
Stay in the Overview tab and rotate through each metric: cost, conversions, conversion value, cost per conversion, ROAS (conversion value ÷ cost), and CTR.
For each metric, note whether it went up, down or sideways and, critically, when the inflection point occurred (e.g., '3 March').
Move to the Campaign tab and work down from the top five spenders, asking which campaign contributed most to the metric change after that date.
Then drop to ad group level (or asset groups in PMax) and repeat the same exercise to see whether all groups moved or one specific group did.
Output two facts: which campaign type fell off, and which specific campaigns and ad groups within it.
caveats: The benefit of a weekly view is trend visibility; a shorter daily view reintroduces the small-sample and latency problems.
The five-minute figure is the speaker's expectation for an experienced operator, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Match failure modes to campaign type: PMax and Shopping
cards.summary: Why identifying the campaign type first matters, and the specific failure modes to check for PMax and Shopping.
cards.use_when: When a Google Ads decline has been traced to a specific campaign and you need to know what to inspect.
steps: Understand that PMax, Shopping and Search decline for different reasons, so establish campaign type before troubleshooting.

PMax / Shopping check 1 — warm/cold drift: check the search term report for brand terms and the audience report for skew toward existing customers. If brand terms are appearing despite exclusions, or the audience skews warm, the exclusion is broken or target ROAS is pushed too high.

PMax / Shopping check 2 — feed health: feed quality drives most Shopping performance (the speaker says 80–90% of PMax performance comes from Shopping). Check products in the campaign for out-of-stock, turned-off or disapproved items, and verify the GMC feed for errors and warnings, including changed titles or descriptions.

PMax / Shopping check 3 — target ROAS: raising tROAS narrows targeting toward warmer, higher-conversion-probability buyers, likely pulling spend back and hurting new-customer acquisition. Cross-check new-customer ROAS in a third-party tool or natively in Google Ads; a higher tROAS typically shows worse NC ROAS.

PMax / Shopping check 4 — product bloat and stock churn: a rapidly growing SKU count flooding one campaign can hurt learning, and high-spend products going in and out of stock reset that product's learning and can affect the whole campaign.
Also check whether spend is being distributed into search partners with poor performance.
caveats: The 80–90% figure is the speaker's stated observation, not a measured benchmark.
Brand exclusion should already be in place — the check is a double-check, not a fix in itself.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Search campaign failure modes: search terms, auction insights, display leakage
cards.summary: Four specific checks for a declining Search campaign, including broad-match reallocation and display leakage.
cards.use_when: When diagnosis points to a Search campaign as the source of a performance decline.
steps: Search terms: split the report either side of the inflection point, sort by spend, and compare the top-spending terms and their efficiency. With broad match and smart bidding, a wild reallocation of spend across terms can be the cause even when overall volume looks similar.
Auction insights: compare before and after the inflection point. A new competitor entering the auction can raise CPCs or reduce your ability to enter auctions at all.
Target ROAS: the same failure mode as PMax — raising tROAS narrows targeting toward warmer buyers rather than magically improving efficiency.
Display leakage: confirm display is turned off for the campaign, or spend may be silently allocated to display, which correlates with the performance drop.
caveats: If search terms and efficiency look materially unchanged either side of the inflection point, move on rather than forcing a conclusion.
The display-leakage check is a specific Google Ads configuration risk; verify the current interface for where display settings live.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Metric decomposition: build the formulas before you touch anything
cards.summary: Every campaign KPI is the product of underlying metrics — learn the decomposition to reach the true root cause rather than the first visible symptom.
cards.use_when: When you've isolated a declining campaign metric and need to trace it down to the trigger that actually moved.
steps: Keep the two core formulas in mind: CPA = CPC ÷ conversion rate, and Clicks = Impressions × CTR. The speaker says these cover roughly 90% of troubleshooting.
At campaign level: attributed revenue is driven by CPC, conversion rate and AOV. Declining conversions come from fewer clicks, lower conversion rate, or broken tracking.

Understand AOV itself decomposes further: it's a blend of new-customer AOV and returning-customer AOV, each sitting on a distribution curve, and each order is mechanically driven by units per transaction and average unit retail.

Use this decomposition to get past superficial answers. Trying to fix AOV by asking 'what offer changed?' is not root cause; drilling into NC AOV, then the distribution curve, then whether UPT or AUR moved, is.
Write out which sub-metric moved and what triggered it before proposing any fix.
caveats: The 90% figure is the speaker's own estimate of coverage from those two formulas.
The speaker says infinite decomposition is possible; the value is choosing the next useful level, not expanding until the trail goes cold.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: CPC troubleshooting: quality score, competition and premium auctions
cards.summary: Three explanations for rising CPC and how to tell whether higher CPC is actually a problem.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing a Google Ads efficiency decline where cost per click has risen.
steps: Add columns for Quality Score, Expected CTR, Ad Relevance and Landing Page Experience at keyword level. Compare before and after the inflection point.
Ad relevance is often the easiest to fix: make the ad copy more relevant to the search terms actually being served.
Expected CTR extrapolates current CTR into the future, so it improves only by making the ads materially better.

Landing page experience is the hardest to change: it requires dev work, and Google's re-crawl/rescoring cadence is unclear — the speaker reports it can take weeks to months even after the site is fixed.
Check auction insights before and after the dip to see if a new competitor entered the auction and is pushing up CPCs.
Consider whether you're now entering premium (more expensive) auctions as a result of a tROAS or bidding change — this is only a problem if those clicks aren't higher quality.
Treat CPC as a near-vanity metric: CPC up with conversion rate up keeps CPA flat and is fine; CPC up with conversion rate flat is the problem signal.
caveats: Landing page experience is presented as occasionally being the bottleneck despite the long, uncertain resync cycle.
Premium auction entry is not automatically bad — judge it on whether conversion rate compensates.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Conversion-rate troubleshooting: tracking, landing page, audience, learning, offer
cards.summary: Five ordered causes of a website conversion rate drop on Google traffic.
cards.use_when: When the conversion-rate leg of the revenue equation has fallen and you need to find which factor is responsible.
steps: Check tracking first: confirm conversion tracking still fires and that you aren't reading the last few days using default conversion columns instead of conversions by conversion time.

Check landing page changes: did the URL change, were prices changed, is a redirect pushing traffic elsewhere, were upsells/cross-sells added, did merchandising shift? The speaker treats this as the number one likely cause of a conversion rate decrease.

Check audience change: same page and site but lower-quality traffic from premium auctions converts worse, and vice versa. Inspect search terms for relevancy to the landing page and whether a bidding-strategy change is pushing toward a different audience.
Check learning phase: a large structural change to the account resets the learning phase, which reliably lowers conversion rates because the system enters the wrong auctions and sends poor traffic.
Check the offer: a promo ended, a discount was removed, or the free shipping threshold changed — all directly affect conversion rate.
caveats: A learning-phase reset from structural change can push you into a feedback loop of decline; avoid causing it unnecessarily.
The ordering reflects the speaker's experience, not a published causal test.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Volume troubleshooting: clicks = impressions × CTR, budget vs bid share loss
cards.summary: How to diagnose a loss of click volume, separating budget constraints from bid/quality constraints.
cards.use_when: When Google Ads efficiency is stable but volume (spend or revenue) has fallen and you need to find why clicks dropped.
steps: Split the click loss into impressions and CTR. Impressions falling means you're entering fewer auctions or your listings show less often.
Distinguish impression share lost to budget from impression share lost to bid. If you're hitting your daily budget cap, more impressions require more spend.
If click volume and impressions are both down while spend has been steady, the speaker says it's almost certainly a bid issue rather than a budget one.
Fix impression share lost to bid by working on its inputs: quality score, new competitors in the auction, and how aggressively you're entering auctions.
If CTR is the falling leg, look at ad fatigue (rare on Google, more plausible on search than Shopping) and audience mismatch — the ad may no longer fit the people and search terms it now serves.
Check ad copy for time mismatch (e.g., a summer sale still running after summer) and, on Shopping, check competitive pricing on the same products.
caveats: Ad fatigue is described as rare on Google, but the speaker allows for it in search ads.
The budget-vs-bid inference relies on spend being stable over the comparison period.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Competitive pricing scripts: pull products rather than match discounts
cards.summary: How a wholesaler used competitor price monitoring to avoid unprofitable Google Shopping auctions.
cards.use_when: When Google Shopping CTR and ROAS fall on specific products and you suspect a competitor has discounted the same items.
steps: Track competitor pricing on your key products in real time — the source describes a script monitoring a major competitor's website for price changes.
When a competitor cuts price materially (the example is 20–30% off), pull or de-prioritise the affected product in the campaign structure rather than continuing to force spend to it.
Rationale: continuing to run the product would mean ROAS falls off a cliff, and matching the discount would erode gross margin to almost nothing.
Use Impression Share lost to rank (search impression share lost {rank}) as the native Google Ads column for this signal.
Reintroduce the product when the competitive discount ends and the price gap closes.
caveats: This is one client example (a sunglasses wholesaler), not a guaranteed result.
Script availability and metric naming may change — verify the current Google Ads interface before building the workflow.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Default to fixes, not rebuilds — and protect the learning phase
cards.summary: Apply targeted fixes and allow time to read them, because a rebuild resets learning and can worsen the decline.
cards.use_when: When you've reached the root cause and are choosing between a targeted change and restructuring the account.
steps: Start with a fix, not a rebuild. Any rebuild triggers a learning reset, which the speaker says will likely put you in a worse position.
Evidence the danger: performance declines, so you make a big change, which causes further decline, which prompts another big change — a feedback loop until the account is in a bad state.
After applying a fix, allow enough time to determine whether it worked before layering another change.
Only if fixes don't work, or clearly won't bridge the gap to historical performance, consider a rebuild.

Before applying, ask honestly how much impact this specific change will make. Changing a headline is unlikely to fix an entire business decline unless a headline change was the original cause. Keep re-thinking the fix until you believe it's strong enough to move the problem area.
caveats: The speaker acknowledges situations dire enough that a 'kitchen sink' response is justified — in that case speed beats clean attribution of the fix.
The threshold for 'enough time' depends on the account's conversion volume, not a fixed window.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Isolate one fix at a time to preserve causal learning
cards.summary: Why applying multiple simultaneous fixes (the kitchen sink) prevents you from knowing what worked — and when to accept that trade-off.
cards.use_when: When deciding how many changes to apply to a landing page, offer or campaign after diagnosing a decline.
steps: Recognise the 'kitchen sink' problem: if you change the offer, redesign the landing page, and adjust traffic continuity all at once and performance recovers, you cannot identify which change mattered.
If the problem recurs later, you'll be unable to solve it without repeating the kitchen sink — you've learned nothing transferable.
Strip back to a smaller set of changes so the outcome is interpretable; this is where the speaker says the strategic judgement lies.
Assess severity first: a dire, urgent decline may justify a kitchen sink because fixing it matters more than knowing why; a mild dip rewards a clean, attributable test.
caveats: Isolating variables slows recovery — the trade-off must be weighed against severity.
This is a principle for interpretability, not a controlled-experiment protocol; the source doesn't specify sample-size or duration requirements.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx

cards.title: Root-cause sentence test: don't touch the account until you can complete it
cards.summary: A gate before making any change — you must be able to state the metric, sub-metric, trigger and root cause in one sentence.
cards.use_when: Before applying any fix to a Google Ads account following a diagnostic process.
steps: Assemble the full chain from the top down: business KPIs → channel checks → campaign types → specific campaign → metric → sub-metric → trigger → root cause.

Check whether you can finish the sentence: 'this campaign is underperforming because this metric dropped, driven by this sub-metric, which was caused by this trigger, which itself was the root cause.'
If you cannot complete that sentence after the process, do not change the account.

Where the client points at a bottom-level metric (e.g., 'CPC is down on this ad'), zoom out first: check business-level KPIs and whether the issue matters to growth. Often it doesn't, and the hour is better spent elsewhere.
caveats: The speaker describes this order of investigation as the skill that separates strong performance marketers from habitual tweakers — it's their opinion, not a formal standard.
The gate can be overridden when a fix is clearly necessary for business continuity.
cards.source_name: How To Fix An Underperforming Google Ads Account.docx
